title: Iterators and generators
summary: Functions that produce values one at a time, pausing in between, so you can work with long or even endless sequences.

sections.heading: Values on demand
body: A generator function (`function*` in JavaScript, any `def` containing `yield` in Python) does not run when you call it. It returns an iterator, and each time a value is asked for, it runs until the next `yield` and hands that value out.
`for...of` / `for...in` loops and spreading (`[...gen]`, `list(gen)`) all ask for values one by one.

sections.heading: Pausing and resuming
body: You can also pull values by hand. Watch the order of the printed lines: the body does not start until the first request, and it pauses at every `yield`.

javascript.code:
function* steps() {
  console.log('starting')
  yield 1
  console.log('resumed')
  yield 2
}
const it = steps()
console.log('created')
console.log(it.next())
console.log(it.next())
console.log(it.next())

python.code:
def steps():
    print('starting')
    yield 1
    print('resumed')
    yield 2

it = steps()
print('created')
print(next(it))
print(next(it))
print(next(it, 'finished'))

sections.heading: Endless sequences
body: Because values are made only when asked for, a generator can go on forever. Take just the part you need and stop.

python.code:
from itertools import islice

def fibonacci():
    a, b = 0, 1
    while True:
        yield a
        a, b = b, a + b

print(' '.join(str(n) for n in islice(fibonacci(), 10)))

sections.heading: A generator can only be used once
body: Once a generator has handed out all its values, it is finished. Looping over it again gives nothing. Call the generator function again for a fresh one.

python.code:
def letters():
    yield 'a'
    yield 'b'

gen = letters()
print(list(gen))
print(list(gen))
print(list(letters()))

mistakes: Calling a generator function and expecting its body to have run.
Reusing a generator that has already been used up.
Spreading or calling `list()` on an endless generator: it never finishes.
